title: Scenarios iter-3: 74 pass, 41 weak, 5 fail
intro: The 40 everyday requests played against a fresh hub with GPT-6 Luna, 3 rep(s) each, a simulated non-technical person answering, judged by a model on each request's Good line. One item per case: give your own verdict and comment where the judge or the agent got it wrong. Total cost $7.070. The full report is .harness-test/scenarios/iter-3/report.md.

items.title: Diagnosis: what the model was shown, why it went that way, and the fixes ranked
items.ask: Are these the right fixes, in the right order? Which would you make first?
items.md:
# Diagnosis: iter-3

Written 2026-11-25T18:28:09.882Z by openai/gpt-6-luna from 120 case rep(s): what the chat model was shown at every step, and why it did what it did. Cost $1.027 (cases $1.011, merging $0.0160).

## Why each step went the way it did

| cause | steps |
|---|---|
| fine | 481 |
| model-error | 167 |
| wrong-mechanism | 42 |
| tool-bug | 32 |
| missing-info | 27 |
| misleading-info | 15 |
| mechanism-missing | 3 |
| mechanism-too-hard | 3 |
| jargon-unexplained | 1 |

**Model arg mistakes** (the model's own call didn't fit and was sent back; not failures in themselves): 4 not recovered, 10 recovered.

## Fixes, ranked by how many case reps they would help

### 1. `context:hub/memory` — 10 case rep(s), confidence 0.84

From [1/r1](rep-1/cases/case-01.md), [1/r2](rep-2/cases/case-01.md), [1/r3](rep-3/cases/case-01.md), [4/r2](rep-2/cases/case-04.md), [7/r2](rep-2/cases/case-07.md), [9/r1](rep-1/cases/case-09.md), [9/r2](rep-2/cases/case-09.md), [9/r3](rep-3/cases/case-09.md), [10/r1](rep-1/cases/case-10.md), [10/r2](rep-2/cases/case-10.md).

**Problem:** The memory guidance does not consistently lead the assistant to save useful, durable personal details shared during a task, or to retain only what is appropriate for future use.

**Proposed:**

> When a person shares a stable personal fact, preference, constraint, ongoing goal, or routine that is likely to help in future chats or repeated requests, save a concise user-scoped memory with `hub__remember`, even if the detail comes up while doing another task. Save only the relevant, durable fact; do not guess, add unrelated personal details, store every form answer or individual log entry, or retain details that are temporary or useful only for the current task. Keep a stated detail limited to the purpose the person gave it rather than inferring broader facts. If it is unclear whether the person wants a detail retained, ask first. Do not save sensitive information unless the person explicitly asks you to remember it, and never save something they ask you not to retain. After saving, continue the current task. Say a memory was saved only after the tool confirms it, and mention it only when helpful. Before asking for personal information or preferences, search memory for relevant details and do not ask again for information already found.

### 2. `system-prompt` — 5 case rep(s), confidence 0.89

From [5/r1](rep-1/cases/case-05.md), [18/r1](rep-1/cases/case-18.md), [18/r2](rep-2/cases/case-18.md), [18/r3](rep-3/cases/case-18.md), [34/r3](rep-3/cases/case-34.md).

**Problem:** The assistant does not consistently check relevant personal information before asking for it, asks for more than it needs, or overstates what personal data it can access.

**Proposed:**

> When an answer depends on personal information, check relevant saved memories and any available source that actually contains that information before asking the person. Do not use a search for available tools as if it searched personal records. If you have not checked a possible source, do not claim it is inaccessible; say what you checked and what you did not. If the information is still missing, say so and ask only for the minimum details needed. If a relevant document could provide them, offer a choice to type or paste the details or attach the document, if attachments are supported; never imply you can access a file that has not been attached. Ask the person not to share secrets or credentials. For private or sensitive information, explain what you can and cannot inspect. If a safe self-service check exists, use web tools to find and read its official instructions, and explain how the person can do it; do not claim you performed a check unless a tool result confirms it. If an optional check needs a non-secret identifier you do not have, explain the self-service option or ask whether they want to provide it without making it a condition for useful guidance. If the person also wants to track the fact, offer a suitable way to record it.

### 3. `system-prompt` — 5 case rep(s), confidence 0.89

From [8/r1](rep-1/cases/case-08.md), [8/r2](rep-2/cases/case-08.md), [12/r1](rep-1/cases/case-12.md), [12/r2](rep-2/cases/case-12.md), [21/r3](rep-3/cases/case-21.md).

**Problem:** Personalized recommendations can be given without first checking relevant memories, clarifying essential constraints, or distinguishing confirmed facts from assumptions.

**Proposed:**

> Before giving a personalized recommendation or plan that depends on a person's preferences, limits, safety needs, or other personal circumstances, search relevant saved memories first with `hub__ctx_search` and `origins: ["memory"]` (for example, `{"text":"relevant preferences and constraints","origins":["memory"]}`). Apply only memories relevant to the request. If an essential detail is not established by memory or the conversation, ask a concise follow-up before making a specific recommendation that depends on it. Prioritize preferences, exclusions, and safety restrictions; ask for other key facts that change suitability, cost, or feasibility. For a time-limited plan, ask how much time is available; when quantities depend on scale, ask how many people or items are involved. For comparisons where variants affect the result, ask which variant is wanted if it is not already known, and use the confirmed variant. Do not replace missing answers with assumptions. You may offer a brief provisional outline, clearly labeled as provisional. Separate stated facts from inferences: label possibilities as such and make advice conditional when it depends on an inference.

### 4. `context:web/guide` — 4 case rep(s), confidence 0.93

From [10/r2](rep-2/cases/case-10.md), [14/r1](rep-1/cases/case-14.md), [14/r2](rep-2/cases/case-14.md), [14/r3](rep-3/cases/case-14.md).

**Problem:** The assistant may rely on details omitted from a partial page, use the wrong tool to read a resource, or fill gaps with assumptions.

**Proposed:**

> Use only details present in content you actually read. For a public webpage URL, use `web__read`; use `hub__resource_read` only with a resource URI returned by the hub or a system. If `web__read` reports a partial or truncated page, omitted characters, or a resource URI and offset, treat the page as incomplete. Before using or saving a fact that may be in the omitted text, read the relevant remaining text with `hub__resource_read` using the returned URI and offset, or read the relevant section from the resource outline. Continue until the needed details appear in content you have read. Do not infer omitted details from a title, snippet, or general knowledge. If you cannot verify a detail, leave it out or say it could not be confirmed. Keep recommendations and opinions separate from factual claims about what a source lists.

### 5. `system-prompt` — 4 case rep(s), confidence 0.89

From [20/r1](rep-1/cases/case-20.md), [24/r1](rep-1/cases/case-24.md), [25/r2](rep-2/cases/case-25.md), [35/r1](rep-1/cases/case-35.md).

**Problem:** The assistant makes unsupported claims about unavailable capabilities or outside-service access, repeats unsuccessful searches, or gives technical next steps without evidence.

**Proposed:**

> Before saying the app cannot do something, check relevant available tools, guides, systems, and settings when the capability may depend on them. For a request involving an outside service or account, first check the systems list. If there is no dedicated system but the API system is available, load `api/guide` and use `api__services` to check whether the service is configured. If it is listed, look for a suitable saved request or documented API operation, and get approval before any change that requires it. If no suitable access or control is available, state only what your checks establish and offer a practical alternative. Do not keep searching the general function list for a missing integration or assume a database contains the service's data. After a targeted search for a function or guide finds no usable match, try at most one different targeted search; if that also fails, stop and say what you could not confirm or do. Do not repeat the same search in later messages without new information or a newly available tool. Explain limitations in everyday words, avoiding technical jargon unless necessary; if a technical term is necessary, explain it in the same sentence. Do not give a technical next step unless available tools or guides establish that it is real and relevant.

### 6. `systems-list` — 4 case rep(s), confidence 0.85

From [2/r1](rep-1/cases/case-02.md), [3/r3](rep-3/cases/case-03.md), [17/r3](rep-3/cases/case-17.md), [23/r3](rep-3/cases/case-23.md).

**Problem:** The systems descriptions do not give an actionable workflow for collecting recurring entries, keeping and updating them, and revisiting them in a persistent view. They also fail to distinguish a form’s collection role from database storage, or a widget’s read-only role from editing.

**Proposed:**

> For information someone wants to keep and revisit, use a database table for the persistent entries. For independently trackable items, store one row per item and include fields for any state that may change. Generate or use database functions to add and update rows. For recurring entries a person will fill in, use a saved input form as the person-facing method when its fields fit; explain it in plain words rather than telling the person to run a database function or exposing its tool name as the ordinary entry method. A form collects answers but does not save them to the table, so use the appropriate database function to store each submitted answer. A plain question is better when only one simple detail is needed; do not make a form when no input is needed. When the person wants a lasting view, consider proposing a widget sourced from a read-only function that returns the relevant rows. A widget can show a table, cards, or a chart; it is a saved view, not an editing tool. Use the source system’s functions to add or change data, and include an update action in the view only if the available functions support row actions. A query used for a totals chart must return the grouped totals itself. A widget proposal is not saved until the person presses Save. For a one-time question or result, do not add a form or widget unless the person asks for one. Use a file for a printable or downloadable copy when requested, or offer it as an extra; do not substitute a static file for an in-app tracker. Do not promise a particular control or interaction unless the proposal supports it.

### 7. `system-prompt` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.93

From [36/r1](rep-1/cases/case-36.md), [36/r2](rep-2/cases/case-36.md), [36/r2](rep-2/cases/case-36.md), [36/r3](rep-3/cases/case-36.md).

**Problem:** The assistant does not reliably check or safely change access controls, may confuse memory with enforcement, and fails to confirm and verify the exact policy scope.

**Proposed:**

> A memory records information for future use; it does not enforce access restrictions. When someone asks to restrict another person's actions, require approval, or change a hub setting, first check whether a relevant control exists, using the function-search tool if needed. Check the requester's authority if it is unclear. Before applying a rule, state the exact people affected, the actions or functions it matches, what it will block or require approval for, and important gaps or harmless actions it may also affect. Ask the person to confirm that specific plan; a broad goal does not confirm a detailed policy they have not seen. Copy actor IDs and rule IDs exactly from tool results; never reconstruct or shorten them. Do not remove existing rules unless you have identified the exact incorrect rule and removal is necessary. After a change, read the current rules and verify each requested person and restriction separately. State only what the final results confirm, including what remains incomplete or unsupported. If no suitable control exists, say what you checked, what it cannot cover, and the closest available option. Keep enough time to report the result, and stop searching once the available controls cannot express the requested scope.

### 8. `system-prompt` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.91

From [2/r2](rep-2/cases/case-02.md), [2/r3](rep-3/cases/case-02.md), [9/r1](rep-1/cases/case-09.md).

**Problem:** The assistant presents internal tool or function names as instructions for the person instead of explaining how to use the app in ordinary language.

**Proposed:**

> When explaining how someone can use something you set up, describe the action in ordinary words and explain what is ready, what still needs approval or a Save action, and what has not been set up. Tool and function names are for your calls, not commands the person must learn. Do not present them as user instructions; mention one only if it is genuinely needed, and explain it. Prefer telling the person what they can type in chat or which user-facing view to open. If a write requires approval, say so.

### 9. `context:hub/saved_fns` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [2/r3](rep-3/cases/case-02.md), [3/r1](rep-1/cases/case-03.md), [3/r2](rep-2/cases/case-03.md).

**Problem:** The tracking guidance does not fully describe how to set up persistent entries, make repeated entry and review convenient, and account for existing history when presenting progress.

**Proposed:**

> For an ongoing log or list, first ensure there is a place that persistently stores the entries, using the appropriate data system (such as a database table). Provide a practical way to add entries and review them, and continue to accept entries in plain language when that is preferred. When someone will repeatedly enter the same typed details, offer a reusable form shown in the chat. A form only collects answers; after submission, use the data system to store the entry and explain any approval required. Do not ask someone to run a database function or copy its arguments unless they specifically request that method. When someone asks to start a log and see progress, first ask whether they have existing entries to include; if so, collect the relevant dates and values before presenting the view. Do not ask for unrelated personal details. Ask for a target only if they want comparisons against one. When someone wants to return to a particular view of the data, use a widget when it improves the workflow: a widget is a lasting chart, table, calendar, or card view over a function that returns a table. Propose it and explain that they must press Save to keep it. Do not create a form or widget merely because a log exists; use these tools when they help with the requested workflow.

### 10. `context:hub/later` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.88

From [26/r1](rep-1/cases/case-26.md), [26/r2](rep-2/cases/case-26.md), [26/r3](rep-3/cases/case-26.md).

**Problem:** Guidance for requests that require a task to happen later or repeatedly does not consistently prompt clarification, a useful action now, or an accurate manual alternative, and may fail to distinguish accessible information from unavailable information or actual app capabilities.

**Proposed:**

> When someone asks for a task or output to happen later or repeatedly, state plainly whether this app can run it or send it at that time. If it cannot, do not imply that a schedule, reminder, shortcut, or external connection has been created. If the request is unclear, ask what the person wants included before producing the result. Offer to do what is feasible now using information you can actually access; check relevant memories when the request depends on previously shared facts or preferences, and say what information you have not checked or cannot access. Use a data source only if it is listed as available and you have checked it; otherwise say it is unavailable here and invite the person to provide the information if they want it included. Give a copy-ready prompt they can use to ask again manually, and, when useful, copy-ready wording for a reminder they can set using an external tool. You may offer to remember a lasting preference if a memory tool is available, but explain that memory does not run a task or create a reminder. If a form feature is available and would genuinely help collect repeated information, explain that the form can be reopened by name but does not fetch data, store answers by itself, run later, or send messages. Do not promise a saved request, shortcut, or other capability unless a tool result confirms it.

### 11. `context:hub/saved_fns` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.88

From [1/r1](rep-1/cases/case-01.md), [1/r2](rep-2/cases/case-01.md), [1/r3](rep-3/cases/case-01.md).

**Problem:** The guidance does not give a reliable, actionable route for turning a request to repeat a check of changing external information into a reusable live check.

**Proposed:**

> When someone wants to repeat a lookup that depends on changing information outside the app, first look for an existing saved fn (a callable tool) that can retrieve it. If none fits, check whether an available system has a suitable documented service and callable source; load the service guide before using it, and do not invent a service, URL, or source. When the source and request can be specified reliably, use the appropriate maker to create and save a reusable request or a small saved program that calls a suitable fn and accepts any inputs that should vary. Use `code__make_code` to save the program when that is the appropriate route. Then call the saved request or program once to get the current result, and explain how to run it again. Do not create a reusable tool for a one-off request when a direct call is enough. A saved fn runs only when called; it does not run on a schedule, monitor changes, or send alerts. If no reliable reusable source or program is available, explain the limitation plainly and offer the nearest option the app supports, such as asking again for an updated lookup.

### 12. `hub-behaviour` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.88

From [27/r1](rep-1/cases/case-27.md), [29/r3](rep-3/cases/case-29.md), [34/r2](rep-2/cases/case-34.md).

**Problem:** Web page access denials and unavailable pages were handled inconsistently, causing failed runs or leaving the assistant without a clear way to use other sources.

**Proposed:**

> When a web read receives HTTP 401 or 403, return a completed result marked unavailable, preserve the attempted URL and status, and clearly state that the page was not read. Do not include page content or retry the same URL automatically. Mark the page inaccessible so the assistant can promptly use other relevant results, preferring accessible official sources and then reliable alternatives; do not treat snippets from unread pages as verified facts. For HTTP 404, likewise mark the page unavailable and offer other relevant results. Suggest rendered retrieval only when the failure indicates a script-rendered or empty page, not for access denial.

### 13. `context:hub/memory` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.86

From [8/r3](rep-3/cases/case-08.md), [14/r3](rep-3/cases/case-14.md), [28/r1](rep-1/cases/case-28.md).

**Problem:** The assistant does not reliably search and apply relevant memories before giving personalized advice or recommendations, especially when the request depends on current circumstances or important restrictions.

**Proposed:**

> Before giving advice, recommendations, or lists that depend on a person's preferences, circumstances, inventory, restrictions, or earlier decisions, search for relevant memories first. Use `hub__ctx_search` with `origins: ["memory"]` when searching for relevant facts. Search before drafting even a provisional personalized answer or asking a follow-up question; do not assume the relevant detail is absent just because the person did not restate it or referred to it unclearly. Read matching memories and load them if needed, then apply them to the answer. For high-consequence restrictions, do not claim an option complies unless its relevant details have been verified; explain what remains unverified and tailor suggestions to the restriction as far as available information allows. If no relevant memory is found, or its meaning is uncertain, ask a brief clarifying question when the missing information is necessary; otherwise, do not assume it.

### 14. `systems-list` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.85

From [22/r1](rep-1/cases/case-22.md), [22/r2](rep-2/cases/case-22.md), [22/r3](rep-3/cases/case-22.md).

**Problem:** The code-system guidance does not fully explain when to create a reusable transformation, how to handle new uploaded inputs, or how to distinguish repeatable processing from persistent storage.

**Proposed:**

> Small saved programs can perform repeatable calculations and transformations of new inputs. The code function can save logic as a program function that takes arguments, may call other functions, and returns a result; it does not store data, read or monitor future uploads by itself, or run automatically. For a process the person expects to repeat, consider making and testing a reusable program function rather than only remembering a preference. For uploaded content, use available resource-reading tools to obtain it and pass suitable content to the program only if the available functions support that workflow. If the input structure must be understood first, ask for one example and inspect it before designing the program. Do not promise that an unfamiliar format can be handled until it has been inspected; if the format or extraction is unsuitable, explain the limitation and offer the closest workable approach. If the person wants records or results kept and looked up across sessions, use a database as well; pair the program with database storage only when database writes work. If writes fail, say that the history is not saved and explain what would need to happen on a later visit. A one-off calculation or a preference about how to answer does not by itself require a saved program or database.

### 15. `hub-behaviour` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.98

From [3/r2](rep-2/cases/case-03.md), [5/r1](rep-1/cases/case-05.md).

**Problem:** The outer tool result reported a different save state from the inner result, causing the assistant to request a redundant save action.

**Proposed:**

> Make the outer tool result report the created item's actual final state. If the inner operation successfully saves it, return an unambiguous saved status and its name, along with instructions for reopening it; do not label it as merely proposed. If no save occurred, return an unambiguous proposed status and identify the action needed to save it. Include one field that distinguishes saved from proposed, and never report both states for the same item.

### 16. `hub-behaviour` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.98

From [15/r1](rep-1/cases/case-15.md), [22/r1](rep-1/cases/case-22.md).

**Problem:** Resource-reading results indicated that text was complete even when passages had been omitted, leaving the assistant without a reliable continuation path.

**Proposed:**

> Make resource-reading results internally consistent. If any text is omitted, cut, or replaced by an omission marker, mark the result partial or truncated and provide an exact offset, section, or usable instruction for continuing the read. Set `truncated: false` only when the returned text is complete. If the requested read can fit the complete resource, return it in full; never report completeness while silently omitting text.

### 17. `hub-behaviour` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.95

From [17/r2](rep-2/cases/case-17.md), [22/r2](rep-2/cases/case-22.md).

**Problem:** Draft validation and saving disagreed: a draft was reported as clean, but saving failed with a generic instruction to fix it, leading to repeated failures.

**Proposed:**

> Make draft validation and saving use the same run check, and ensure the save stage receives and executes the exact draft validated earlier, including drafts with multi-row inserts. If a draft is reported as clean, saving must accept it or return the specific validation or execution error and exact correction needed. Preserve actual failure details; never tell the assistant a draft is clean and then return a generic instruction to fix it. Stop after a repeated identical save failure and do not invite an unchanged retry.

### 18. `context:input/basics` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.94

From [7/r2](rep-2/cases/case-07.md), [7/r3](rep-3/cases/case-07.md).

**Problem:** The assistant asked for several needed details in free text instead of using the available form tool.

**Proposed:**

> When you need several details that only the person can provide before you can make a useful plan or recommendation, use `input__get_input` to ask the few essential questions together in one form. Do not replace the form with a list of questions in your reply just because the request feels conversational. A form is a set of typed fields shown in the chat; describe each field and whether it is required. The form definition is saved so it can be shown again, but the form itself does not store the answers. After showing a form, end your turn and wait for the person's next message with their answers. For one quick conversational detail, ask in your reply; if one typed answer must be collected in a structured format, use a one-question form. Do not use a form when no information is missing.

### 19. `context:web/guide` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.93

From [4/r1](rep-1/cases/case-04.md), [10/r3](rep-3/cases/case-10.md).

**Problem:** Recommendation searches lack a firm stopping rule, leading to repeated searches and unnecessary page reads.

**Proposed:**

> For recommendations, first decide whether current or independently verified information is needed. Use your knowledge for ordinary descriptive reasons; search when the person asks for current or sourced information, or when you need to verify a specific claim. For a request involving a few options within a specified area and time range, begin with one focused basic search using the confirmed constraints. Review its results before making at most one targeted refinement; use advanced search only if basic results do not find useful pages. Keep the search focused on a few candidates, prefer authoritative listings when relevant, and read at most two useful pages total. Stop when you can provide the requested number of options and a short supported reason for each. If a page fails, try one alternative source for that fact; do not repeat searches or read more pages for facts already established.

### 20. `system-prompt` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.93

From [22/r2](rep-2/cases/case-22.md), [37/r1](rep-1/cases/case-37.md), [37/r1](rep-1/cases/case-37.md).

**Problem:** The assistant does not reliably verify arithmetic or batch counts, and may create a saved program for a one-time calculation instead of calculating directly.

**Proposed:**

> For a one-time calculation, work from the values already available; do not create or search for a saved program unless the person wants to reuse the calculation. Before writing a batch of rows, count the supplied rows and check that the count matches the requested count. Verify computed totals against the source values before saving or reporting them; do not rely on an unverified mental calculation or guess how many records fit a rough category. If the result is too large to total reliably, retrieve a smaller, manageable set and state clearly that the subtotal covers only that set. If the source, count, or values are ambiguous or incomplete, resolve that first or say you cannot total it reliably instead of inventing a figure.

### 21. `context:hub/earlier_chats` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [29/r1](rep-1/cases/case-29.md), [29/r2](rep-2/cases/case-29.md).

**Problem:** Earlier-chat guidance does not require checking a conversation’s timestamp against the person’s stated timeframe and the current local date or time, which can lead to an unsupported claim about when the conversation happened.

**Proposed:**

> When a person asks about an earlier conversation from a particular or relative timeframe, compare the conversation’s timestamp with the current local date and time when both are available. Do not state that it happened in the requested timeframe unless the timestamp supports that. If the timestamp conflicts, briefly note the discrepancy; if it is unavailable or unclear, say you cannot verify the timing rather than guessing. Identify the conversation by its title when available, then answer the request using the messages you read without claiming an unsupported timeframe.

### 22. `context:hub/policies` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [36/r2](rep-2/cases/case-36.md), [36/r3](rep-3/cases/case-36.md).

**Problem:** The prompt did not explain how policies, approvals, and budgets differ or how to choose and communicate a policy’s scope. It also lacked guidance for identifying the functions that perform a restricted action without blocking unrelated functions, and for explaining coverage limits.

**Proposed:**

> ## Access and approval policies
> A policy controls whether a person may run a matching function: it can allow the run, deny it, or require approval before it proceeds. A function is a tool. Policy targets may specify a person and, where supported, a named function, a system, or a function kind. A rule for one function does not cover other functions merely because they have similar effects. Use `hub__policies_list` to inspect existing rules and `hub__set_policy` to add a rule. Use `hub__remove_rule` to remove a rule only when that change is requested or confirmed.
> 
> Before changing access, explain the exact scope in plain language and use the narrowest reliable target the controls support. Never use an empty or broad target as a substitute for a restriction the controls cannot express. For a request to prevent a type of action, identify the functions that actually perform that action and inspect their descriptions. Do not block unrelated functions just because they belong to the same system or make some change. If you cannot reliably identify every matching action, state the exact limited coverage before asking for confirmation; do not imply that the requested scope is fully enforced.
> 
> A rule for a function kind applies to every matching function, including harmless functions and functions added later. Explain that tradeoff. An approval applies only before a covered action runs. A budget limits hub-measured usage or run cost; it is not a general detector or approval gate for charges or payments handled by an outside service. No policy or budget guarantees coverage for actions that do not pass through a matching function. If the available controls cannot express the requested scope, say so rather than implying full coverage.

### 23. `context:web/guide` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [12/r3](rep-3/cases/case-12.md), [29/r3](rep-3/cases/case-29.md).

**Problem:** Web-based claims may rely on snippets or unread content, and citations may not identify every page actually used.

**Proposed:**

> For every factual claim based on web research, use only information confirmed in the text of a page you read. Before stating a precise value or other specific detail, make sure it appears in that page text; a search snippet or short answer is not enough. Cite the exact `finalUrl` returned by `web__read`; do not construct, guess, or substitute a URL from memory. Include a URL for every page used to support a claim, either alongside the claim or in a short sources list. Do not imply that an unread page supports a claim. If a page does not confirm a detail, say it remains unverified and do not present it as fact.

### 24. `system-prompt` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [38/r1](rep-1/cases/case-38.md), [38/r3](rep-3/cases/case-38.md).

**Problem:** When asked what it can do, the assistant gives an unhelpful feature catalog or hedges about capabilities that the systems list establishes.

**Proposed:**

> When someone asks what you can do, base your answer on the `<systems>` list in this prompt, which names the systems available in this chat. Give a short, friendly overview with two or three concrete, everyday examples drawn from different useful capabilities; do not list every system or tool. Do not say a listed capability is available only conditionally. If a specific account, service, file, or dataset needs checking, distinguish that from the system's general capability and check it before promising access. Mention relevant limitations stated in the prompt and invite the person to choose a task.

### 25. `tool-description:hub/add_user` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [35/r1](rep-1/cases/case-35.md), [35/r3](rep-3/cases/case-35.md).

**Problem:** The description does not distinguish account creation from setting up sign-in or sending an invitation, which can lead to unsupported claims about how the added account can sign in.

**Proposed:**

> Add an account with its access level and groups. This creates the account only; it does not send an email, invitation, password-setup link, or sign-in instructions. A successful result, whether it returns an identifier or confirms the account was added, does not establish the sign-in method or confirm that an invitation was sent. Do not infer either from an email address or successful creation. Use this for requests to add an account. Assign the lowest access level that meets the request and explain what that level allows. Do not claim the account can complete sign-in until a result or guide confirms the sign-in method.

### 26. `system-prompt` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.89

From [6/r3](rep-3/cases/case-06.md), [12/r1](rep-1/cases/case-12.md).

**Problem:** The assistant repeats tool or guide discovery and loading, or chooses a tool that does not match the task.

**Proposed:**

> Choose tools according to the task: use `web__search` to find public webpages and `web__read` to inspect a page; use `hub__fns_search` only to find callable tools. Before using a system, load its guide once. If the guide is already in your prompt and the needed tool is available, use them directly. Before loading a function, check whether it is already in your tools; a loaded function remains available for the rest of the chat, including after another message, so call it directly rather than loading it again.

### 27. `system-prompt` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.89

From [23/r1](rep-1/cases/case-23.md), [23/r2](rep-2/cases/case-23.md).

**Problem:** The assistant treats static text or Markdown checkboxes as an interactive checklist, or fails to create persistent tracking when ongoing updates are requested.

**Proposed:**

> When someone asks for a list or chart they need to mark as done, update, or revisit over time, treat it as ongoing tracking even if they do not explicitly say to save it. Use a database table to keep the items and their changing state, and use a widget when they need a view they can open again. A database is a table of lasting rows; a widget is a saved view of rows. Follow the database and widget guides, and use an update action only when the widget and source support it. A text answer may be enough for a one-time display or printable template. Never present a text table as an interactive checklist or describe text, Markdown, or emoji symbols as controls. Say an item can be checked, changed, saved, or updated only when a tool result shows the app provides that action. Label any static text layout as static and do not imply its symbols record changes.

### 28. `context:api/guide` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.88

From [24/r1](rep-1/cases/case-24.md), [24/r2](rep-2/cases/case-24.md).

**Problem:** The guide does not clearly distinguish an empty service lookup from account-connection status, or prohibit unsupported claims about enabling or setting up a service.

**Proposed:**

> If a lookup for services available to this chat returns no matching service, say that no matching service is configured for use here. Do not treat that result as checking whether the person connected an account or the status of a separate account-connection setting. If the person says they connected an account, verify it using an available connection-status capability when possible; otherwise, state that you cannot verify it. A service configured for requests and a connected account are separate: signing in is possible only when a supported integration exists. Do not claim an administrator can enable a service, direct the person to a settings page, or promise access unless loaded guidance or a tool result confirms those steps. If the available information does not explain how to add an integration, say so rather than guessing.

### 29. `context:hub/undo` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.88

From [30/r2](rep-2/cases/case-30.md), [30/r3](rep-3/cases/case-30.md).

**Problem:** The undo guidance discourages using the available undo tool for earlier actions and does not clearly explain how to handle a request to undo a recent action. This can lead the assistant to make manual changes instead of using undo or to claim effects were reversed without confirmation.

**Proposed:**

> ## Undo
> When someone asks you to undo an action, use `hub__turn_undo` for the turn that made that action, when the turn can be identified and the tool can undo its effects. Do not manually recreate or reverse the effects first, or describe a manual change as an undo. A turn identifier is required. If you cannot identify the relevant turn, do not guess or make a replacement change; explain that you cannot identify it and ask which recent action they mean. If the tool cannot undo the action, say plainly what prevents the undo. You may offer a manual reversal only as a separate alternative. The tool reports what it reversed, what it could not reverse, and any changes left in place; describe those results accurately and never promise more than the result confirms. Undo may also remove the turn from the chat, so mention this when relevant.

### 30. `context:web/guide` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.88

From [11/r2](rep-2/cases/case-11.md), [11/r3](rep-3/cases/case-11.md).

**Problem:** Advice may depend on an unconfirmed circumstance, and recommendations may fail to compare feasible alternatives or explain trade-offs.

**Proposed:**

> When a source gives different advice for different circumstances, do not silently assume which circumstance applies. Ask if the distinction changes the recommendation; otherwise choose the safer guidance that applies across the unresolved cases and explain why. When asked to choose the easiest or best option, briefly compare the relevant alternatives using verified information, name the main trade-offs, and recommend one. Do not imply that you checked a detail you did not verify or invent comparisons. If the available information is insufficient for a fair comparison, say what remains unknown.

From [30/r2](rep-2/cases/case-30.md), [30/r3](rep-3/cases/case-30.md).

**Problem:** The assistant could not reliably identify the target for an undo request because the tool required a turn identifier that was not available in the conversation or suggestion.

items.ask: Is the judge right? What should it have done?
items.md:
**Request:** "Can I get a way to keep track of the weather and get a heads-up when tomorrow's supposed to rain?"

**Good:** Asks where they live (or uses what it knows), builds a reusable weather check, shows tomorrow's forecast, and is honest that it can't yet message them on its own.

Mean 5.3/10 · same verdict every rep · $0.0491

### rep 1: weak 5/10

The assistant asked for the location, checked a forecast, and clearly explained that it cannot send alerts on its own. But its forecast appears to mix Thursday-night rain with Friday’s high temperature, and it didn’t save the location or set up a reusable weather check.

- ✓ Asked for the city or ZIP code before checking.
- ✓ Clearly stated it cannot monitor the weather or send a later alert.
- ✓ Provided useful, sourced iPhone instructions for precipitation notifications.
- ✗ Reported rain all day Thursday and a high near 44°F, while the search results distinguish Thursday-night rain from Friday’s high of 44°F.
- ✗ Did not save the location or otherwise establish a reusable weather check.

Cause **hallucinated**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: Ground the forecast in the source’s specific day and time period, and save the user’s location for future weather checks.

3 turns · 17 runs · 11 model calls · hub $0.0206 · person $0.0006 · 66s · ended: satisfied (I got the forecast for tomorrow and a straight answer that it can't send alerts by itself, plus how to set up alerts on my iPhone.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 2, the model had the person’s location in the new message but reasoned, “The user hasn’t provided a city or region here,” and failed to save that useful lasting fact. At step 7, the NWS search result explicitly separated Thursday-night rain from Friday’s high near 44°F, while the page read at step 6 warned that its forecast text was partial and not to state what was omitted. The model nevertheless combined those details into an unsupported all-day Thursday forecast. The prompt also explained that API requests can be saved for fresh data and that memories can retain relevant personal facts, but the model did neither. It correctly stated that it cannot send alerts itself, and its later iPhone instructions were sourced and appropriately limited to next-hour precipitation alerts.

- `context:hub/memory` (0.84): The memory guidance says to remember lasting facts that matter later, but does not make the value of retaining a location supplied for recurring local lookups explicit.
  > When a person gives a stable personal detail that will help with future requests—such as their usual location for local information—save it as a user memory if it is relevant to an ongoing or repeat-use request. Do not save a temporary location or a detail that is not useful later. Use the detail the person already gave; do not ask for it again unless it is missing or unclear.
- `context:hub/saved_fns` (0.77): The model did not turn a request for repeat access to fresh external information into a reusable check, despite being told that saved API requests can fetch fresh data when run again.
  > When a person wants to repeat a lookup for fresh information from outside the app, do not treat a web search or a saved web page as a reusable live check. First search for a saved fn (a callable tool) that already does it. If none fits, check whether the API system has a suitable service; load its guide before using it, and use its maker to create and then run a saved request when the service and documented endpoint allow it. If no suitable live request can be made, explain that limitation and offer the closest real option, such as asking them to return and request an updated lookup. A saved request runs only when called; it does not run on a schedule or send alerts by itself.
- `context:web/guide` (0.94): The guide says to verify details on the read page, but does not explicitly warn against combining a nighttime forecast with the following day’s temperature or describing a limited period as an all-day forecast.
  > For forecasts and other time-based information, keep each claim tied to the exact date and period stated by the source. Do not turn a nighttime forecast into an all-day forecast, or attach a temperature from one day to a different day or period. If the page is partial, follow its instruction to read the omitted section before making a claim about it. When the source does not establish the requested date or period, say what it does establish and what remains unconfirmed.

### rep 2: weak 6/10

The assistant asked for the location, checked and shared a forecast, and clearly said it cannot send automatic alerts. But it only suggested returning to the chat rather than saving a reusable weather check or the location for future use.

- ✓ Asked for the town or ZIP instead of guessing.
- ✓ Shared a forecast with a source link.
- ✓ Was clear that it cannot send texts or phone notifications automatically.
- ✗ Did not save the location or create a reusable weather check for later.

Cause **missed-capability**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: Save Columbus 43214 as the location for a reusable weather check, then explain that the user can return to it for an updated forecast but cannot receive automatic alerts.

2 turns · 8 runs · 6 model calls · hub $0.0097 · person $0.0006 · 38s · ended: satisfied (The assistant was straight that it can't send automatic alerts, and I can come back to this chat to re-check the forecast, which is what I wanted.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 6, the model stopped after offering a manual return to the chat, even though the prompt said under “Nothing runs later” to offer “a saved fn the person can run when the time comes,” explained that saved programs can call other fns, and instructed it to remember lasting details that will matter again. The model’s own reasoning recognized that a saved check could help, but it did not save the detail or attempt to build one. The limitation on automatic notifications was handled correctly; the missed opportunity was making the closest reusable option.

- `context:hub/saved_fns` (0.86): The guidance describes saved fns generally but does not give a concrete route for a recurring request that needs fresh information. The model recognized a reusable check might help but did not turn that into an action.
  > For a request the person expects to repeat using fresh information, consider making a reusable fn rather than only telling them to ask again. First find a suitable fn that can retrieve the information. If a saved code program can call that fn and return a useful result, use `code__make_code` to save a small program with the inputs that should vary, then call the saved program once for the current result. Do not use this for a one-off request when a direct call is enough, and do not imply the saved fn runs on a timer or sends notifications. If no suitable source fn or reusable program is available, explain that and offer the nearest option the app actually supports.
- `context:hub/memory` (0.90): The existing memory guidance is general, and the model did not save a lasting detail the person supplied for future use.
  > When a person supplies a lasting personal detail that will help with a request they want to repeat, save that fact with `hub__remember` using `scope: "user"`, unless they say it is temporary or do not want it remembered. Save only the relevant fact, not a guess or extra personal details. Tell the person it was saved only after the tool confirms it.
- `context:code/basics` (0.79): The code guidance emphasizes calculations and small pieces of logic, which may leave a reusable current-information check seeming outside the intended use, despite programs being able to call other fns.
  > A saved code program can also be a small reusable workflow when it can call suitable existing fns. For a repeat request that needs fresh information, use it only if the program can call a source fn that retrieves that information; describe the inputs, the result, and which fn it should call. Then call the saved program once to get the current result. A code program is not a scheduler: it runs only when called and cannot send a future alert.

- `context:hub/Memory` (0.78): The memory guidance does not distinguish a place supplied for one lookup from a place clearly intended as the default for future repeated lookups.
  > When a person gives a place as the default for repeated requests, and their wording makes continued use clear, save a user-scoped memory that describes it only as their chosen lookup location for that purpose. Do not assume it is their home or save a one-time location as a lasting fact. If it is unclear whether they want the place retained, ask before saving. Memories are not automatically present in a new chat: search for relevant memories before relying on them.

items.md:
**Request:** "I keep forgetting what I spend on groceries. Can you help me keep track?"

**Good:** Sets up somewhere to log trips, makes adding one easy, offers a monthly view.

Mean 6.7/10 · verdicts differ · $0.583

### rep 1: weak 6/10

The assistant created a grocery log, saved the Nov 14 Kroger trip, and provided a working November total and month-by-month summary. But it didn’t set up the input form or widget that would make logging and viewing trips easier, and the setup took many tool steps.

- ✓ Saved the trip with the date, store, and amount the person provided.
- ✓ Created a saved monthly summary and correctly reported November’s total as $172.48.
- ✓ Confirmed the person could add trips conversationally and ask for totals later.
- ✗ Did not use an input form or widget for easier trip entry and viewing.
- ✗ A draft for the monthly summary failed before the assistant recovered with a working query.

Cause **missed-capability**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: Look for and use the available input form and widget capabilities alongside the database log, so adding trips and viewing monthly totals are easy.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (1 of 31 tool calls failed or were refused: draft (tool-error); apart: 1 model arg mistake, recovered (the model's own call sent back to fix; not failures))

4 turns · 31 runs · 26 model calls · hub $0.154 · person $0.0015 · 110s · ended: satisfied (The app now logs each grocery trip and shows the November total, which is exactly what I wanted.)

**Diagnosis:** The main gap was not that the app lacked the needed tools: step 1 exposed `input__get_input` and `widgets__make_widget`, and the prompt explained that forms can be saved and widgets provide lasting views. At steps 7–8 the assistant nevertheless chose conversational entry alone, and at steps 22–23 it finished without a widget, so the setup missed the requested ease of logging and persistent monthly view. Separately, at step 22 it reopened an explicit date after the trip had already been saved; the relative-date discrepancy should have been resolved before writing, if clarification was needed. The monthly-query agent also made an unsupported date-function draft at step 18 and an invalid draft call at step 19, but recovered and produced a working query.

- `systems-list` (0.86): The systems descriptions explain forms, databases, and widgets individually, but do not make the combined workflow for a repeatable log and a lasting view sufficiently actionable. The assistant defaulted to conversational entry and stopped after creating a query.
  > For a request to keep a structured log or list that will receive entries repeatedly, use a database table for the lasting entries. When a reusable structured entry screen would make adding entries easier, create a saved form with the input system; the form collects answers but does not save them to the table, so use the database functions to store each answer. When the person wants to return to a persistent view, use the widgets system with a read-only table-returning function as its source. A query that groups and totals rows must already return those grouped totals before it can be used as a totals chart. The person must save a widget proposal before it is kept. Use only the parts that fit the request; a one-time question or result does not need a saved form or widget.
- `system-prompt` (0.83): The prompt says not to invent missing dates, but does not explicitly say how to handle a relative date that conflicts with an explicitly provided calendar date. The assistant saved the date and then asked whether to replace it.
  > If a relative date phrase and an explicit calendar date appear to conflict, do not choose one silently and do not write the entry yet. Ask one concise question to resolve the conflict before making the change. Once the person confirms an explicit date, keep that date unless they later ask to change it.
- `fn-instructions:database/author_query` (0.73): The query-authoring agent tried a date-formatting function that the database rejected at execution, although it had access to `query_syntax`; the failure added an avoidable draft attempt.
  > For expressions involving dates, use only date functions and argument shapes shown by `query_syntax` for the loaded database. Do not assume a function from another SQL dialect is available. If the draft reports an unknown function, replace that expression with a supported function from `query_syntax` before drafting again.

The assistant created a simple trip form, logged the $172.48 Kroger trip, and saved a monthly total card that showed November’s spending. It initially gave confusing technical tool names, but adapted when the user asked for a simpler setup.

- ✓ Saved a monthly total card and verified it showed $172.48.

3 turns · 82 runs · 57 model calls · hub $0.244 · person $0.0007 · 169s · ended: satisfied (They now have a simple trip form and a monthly total card showing $172.48, which is what they asked for.)

**Diagnosis:** The needed guidance was already present at step 1: the prompt said to write plainly, explained that forms collect typed answers and can be reused, and described databases as a way to keep entries over time. At step 31, the assistant nevertheless exposed internal function names and gave only database functions as the way to add an entry, making the setup confusing and prompting the person to ask for a simpler form. Once asked, the assistant used the form and widget mechanisms appropriately; the query-authoring argument error at step 39 was corrected and did not prevent the successful result.

- `system-prompt` (0.94): The prompt says to write plainly, but it does not explicitly forbid presenting internal tool/function identifiers as the person's instructions. Step 31 exposed raw names rather than explaining how to use the log.
  > When explaining a setup to the person, describe actions in ordinary words, such as “fill in the entry form” or “open the saved view.” Do not show internal tool or function names as user instructions; those names are for your calls, not the person's interface. If the person asks how to run a saved function, explain the available user-facing way to open it rather than assuming they can use its technical name.
- `context:database/basics` (0.85): The database guidance explains how to make a table and its ready-made functions, but does not make the form-plus-database pattern prominent for repeated entries with several typed fields. That leaves the model with a technical database function as the apparent entry method.
  > For a repeated log or list where each entry needs several typed details, use a database table to keep the entries and a saved form to collect each new entry. A form asks questions; it does not save its answers by itself, so after the person submits it, use the table's add-entry function. Explain this in plain language, not by listing function names. For a person who only wants a place to store entries and is comfortable using the available functions, a form is not always necessary. If they want to revisit a summary or chart, use a saved widget over a query that returns the appropriate totals.

When the person wants to return to a particular view of the data, use a widget: a widget is a lasting chart, table, calendar, or card view over a function that returns a table. Propose it and explain that the person must press Save to keep it. Do not create a form or widget merely because a log exists; use them when they improve the requested workflow.

**Request:** "Track my daughter's reading minutes every night and show me how she's doing."

**Good:** A quick way to log a night, a chart over time.

Mean 7.7/10 · same verdict every rep · $0.597

### rep 1: pass 8/10

The assistant set up a reusable nightly entry form, saved the three supplied entries, and created a chart showing all three nights together. It was clear that it cannot prompt the user automatically each night.

- ✓ Created a form and database-backed reading log.
- ✓ Added the Nov 18–20 entries and verified all three appear in the chart.
- ✓ Saved a bar chart with date-range controls.
- ✗ The chart opens to the selected Nov 18–20 range, so later entries may require adjusting the range to appear.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (1 of 77 tool calls failed or were refused: widgets/make_widget (failed); apart: 2 model arg mistakes, 1 recovered, 1 not (the model's own call sent back to fix; not failures))

5 turns · 77 runs · 47 model calls · hub $0.183 · person $0.0027 · 174s · ended: satisfied (The nightly entry form is set up and the saved chart shows all three reading nights together.)

**Diagnosis:** The initial setup at step 24 followed the prompt’s general tracking guidance but did not ask whether there was history to import, so the first progress view was empty. After the entries were added, the widget agent at step 43 chose fixed date defaults despite its own instruction that dates can be relative so saved views stay current. Step 47 then confirmed the three-night preview without warning that later entries may fall outside that fixed range. The setup and data claims were otherwise backed by tool results, and the chart preview verified all three supplied entries.

- `context:hub/saved_fns` (0.84): The tracking guidance says to provide a way to add entries and a way to see them, but does not say to ask about existing history when the person also asks to see progress. The assistant therefore presented an empty chart before collecting past entries.
  > When someone asks to start an ongoing log and see progress, first ask whether they have existing entries they want included. If they do, collect the dates and values needed to add them before presenting the progress view. Do not ask for unrelated personal details. Ask for a target only if the person wants comparisons against a target; otherwise, set up the log and view without one.
- `fn-instructions:widgets/make_widget` (0.88): The instructions mention relative dates but do not set a default for ongoing trackers. Fixed literal range defaults can make a saved view omit later entries, and the final answer did not explain that limitation.
  > For an ongoing tracker or progress view, use date-range defaults that keep the view current: default the end date to today, and start at the earliest date being tracked or another suitably broad start. Use relative dates where supported. If the person explicitly requests a fixed historical window, keep that window and tell them that entries outside it will not appear until they extend the range. Do not imply that a fixed-range view will include later entries.
- `tool-description:widgets/make_widget` (0.78): The call supplied `args` as a list of `{key, value}` objects and a nonexistent widget name. The tool description already says `args` is an object, but a compact contrast can help avoid repeating this shape error.
  > For `args`, pass one JSON object keyed by the source argument names, such as `{"start":"2025-01-01","end":"2025-01-31"}`. Do not pass a list of `{key, value}` objects or a JSON string. When creating a new widget, leave `widget` out; include `widget` only to change an existing widget whose name is known from a tool result.

items.title: 4. Books read — weak/pass/pass
items.ask: Is the judge right? What should it have done?
items.md:
**Request:** "Keep a list of the books I've read and tell me what I should read next."

**Good:** Starts the list, asks a few books to start from, gives suggestions with reasons.

Mean 8.0/10 · verdicts differ · $0.413

### rep 1: weak 6/10

The assistant saved all four titles, remembered the reading preferences, and gave three relevant picks with reasons. But the recommendation work took 83 tool calls and 208 seconds, far more than needed for this request.

- ✓ Created a persistent book list and added all four titles.
- ✓ Asked for books and preferences instead of guessing.
- ✓ Saved the user's tastes and gave three tailored recommendations with reasons.
- ✗ Spent 208 seconds and made many unnecessary research calls; failed page reads were worked around.

Cause **slow**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: Streamline recommendations: use a small number of targeted searches and avoid repeatedly verifying straightforward book descriptions.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (2 of 83 tool calls failed or were refused: web/read (failed); apart: no model arg mistakes)

3 turns · 83 runs · 44 model calls · hub $0.228 · person $0.0010 · 208s · ended: satisfied (My books are saved and I got three picks with reasons, which is exactly what I wanted.)

**Diagnosis:** The list-building and preference-memory steps worked. The excessive time came from the follow-up research loop at steps 29 and 31–42: despite `web/guide` saying to pick “the one or two best results,” the assistant kept changing candidates, searching for more books, and revisiting sources after it already had enough information. The 403 results at steps 33 and 38 were ordinary page-access failures, and the tool advice to try another result was reasonable; the problem was continuing broad research beyond that fallback. The final claims and links were supported by pages that had been read.

- `context:web/guide` (0.91): The guide recommends one or two pages but does not set a practical stopping rule for recommendation requests, so the assistant kept searching and verifying additional candidates.
  > For recommendations, first decide whether current or independently verified information is actually needed. Use your knowledge for ordinary descriptive reasons, and use web search when the person asks for current or sourced information, or when you need to verify a specific claim. If you browse, keep the search focused on the few candidates you may recommend; read at most two useful pages total. Stop when you can give the requested number of recommendations and a short supported reason for each. If a page fails, try one alternative source for that fact; do not repeat searches or read more pages for facts already established.
- `tool-description:web/search` (0.78): The search description does not discourage repeated candidate exploration after a useful result set has already been found.
  > For a request for a small set of recommendations, prefer one focused query that can return several relevant candidates. Do not keep searching for new candidates once you have enough plausible options; search again only to resolve a specific uncertainty that affects the answer. Search results are leads, not pages you have read.

### rep 1: pass 8/10

The assistant asked for the missing date, recorded the estimated change and next-due date, and clearly explained that it cannot send reminders or add calendar events. It created a useful log as the closest available alternative.

- ✓ Asked for the last-change date rather than guessing.
- ✓ Saved the estimated date, filter size, interval, and Nov 3, 2026 due date in the database.
- ✓ Clearly stated that automatic notifications, recurring calendar events, and scheduled emails are unavailable.
- ✗ Its directions about saving the proposed widget were a little confusing, since the run shows the widget was already saved.

5 turns · 33 runs · 26 model calls · hub $0.200 · person $0.0017 · 124s · ended: satisfied (Automatic reminders aren't possible here and the assistant has been straight about that; the filter log now holds the due date, which is as close as the app gets to what I wanted.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 1, the prompt already said to ask only for essential missing details, but the model broadened a simple date question into requests for a model, measurements, or a photo. The useful initial answer at step 6 corrected course by asking for the date and offering to record it. The main confusion came at step 20: the widget maker’s inner result said “Saved widgets/furnace_filter_changes,” while the outer `widgets__make_widget` result said “Proposed, not saved.” The assistant followed the conflicting outer result and repeated that mistaken save instruction at step 26, even though the widget had been saved.

- `system-prompt` (0.82): Although the prompt says “Ask only what you need, the essentials first,” the model suggested several extra details when only the missing date was needed.
  > When a person asks about a past personal fact, first check the relevant saved information. If it is not there, say you do not know and ask only for the detail needed to answer. Do not request related details, photos, or background unless they are necessary for the person’s actual request. If the person also indicates they want to keep track of this kind of fact, offer a suitable way to record it.
- `hub-behaviour` (0.98): The widget maker’s inner result said “Saved widgets/furnace_filter_changes,” but the outer `widgets__make_widget` result said “Proposed, not saved,” leaving the assistant with a false save status.
  > Make the outer `widgets__make_widget` result report the widget maker’s actual final state. If the inner agent successfully calls `offer` and returns a saved widget, return that saved status and its name; do not return “Proposed, not saved.” If no save occurred, return the proposal status. Include one unambiguous field that distinguishes `saved` from `proposed`.

Mean 7.3/10 · verdicts differ · $0.409

### rep 1: pass 8/10

The assistant asked about the right factors, gave a gentle three-day beginner plan, and set up a run log the person can use with natural-language entries. It was clear that it cannot send reminders automatically and disclosed that saving may require approval.

- ✓ Asked about running experience, goal, schedule, and health considerations in one form.
- ✓ Provided a gradual plan with walk breaks and sensible guidance for easing off or repeating a week.
- ✓ Created a database-backed run log and offered simple phrases to add and view runs.
- ✓ Clarified that automatic reminders are not available.
- ✗ Initially suggested long tool names as the way to log runs, which the person found confusing; it corrected course when asked.

**Diagnosis:** The plan and database setup worked, and the app had the tools needed for the requested workflow. At step 10, the model did not follow the memory guidance already in the prompt—“Remember when the person asks you to, or tells you a lasting fact or preference that will matter again”—for the goal and schedule relevant to future check-ins. At step 19, it exposed the saved-function names as the way to log and view runs, although the person wanted a quick, ordinary chat interaction; the prompt did not explicitly say to keep those names internal. The person had to correct that at step 20. Finally, at step 21, the result explicitly said to answer from the rows, but the model repeated the same read before answering.

- `system-prompt` (0.90): The model presented technical saved-function names as the way the person had to add and view entries. The prompt says to write plainly, but does not explicitly distinguish the assistant's function calls from how the person can ask in chat.
  > Function names are for your tool calls, not commands the person must learn. When a person wants to add or view something, explain the ordinary words they can type in chat and use the relevant tools yourself. For example, say they can write “add a task: review the notes” or “show my tasks”; do not tell them to call a function by its technical name unless they ask how to use functions directly. If a write requires approval, explain that approval may be needed.
- `context:hub/memory` (0.74): The existing memory guidance covers lasting facts, but the model did not retain the person's ongoing goal and schedule for future support.
  > For ongoing plans or accountability requests, consider whether a goal, schedule, or preference the person has shared will help in later chats. If it is likely to matter again, save a brief, non-sensitive memory at user scope. Save only what is useful for future help, not every detail; do not store sensitive health information unless the person asks you to remember it.
- `system-prompt` (0.86): The model repeated a successful read even though the result explicitly instructed it to answer from the returned data.
  > Use a tool result when it already answers the question. Do not repeat a successful read just to confirm the same information; make another call only if the result is incomplete, stale for the request, or the person asks you to check again.

But it also presented a Worthington Farmers Market and a model-railroad open house with a calendar link that, in the transcript, leads to a different event—so some recommendations weren’t reliably supported.

**Diagnosis:** The assistant correctly asked for the location, used the web system, and continued after the 403. The reliability failure came when it stopped matching claims to the page actually cited: at step 14 it called the “Sunday Funday: Holiday Open House” calendar entry a Saturday farmers market, and at step 20 it reused that same event link for the model railroad open house. At step 18 the search output itself mixed a “Third Thursday Night Market” title with model railroad details, but the assistant should have treated that mismatch as a cue to verify the event-specific page; at step 19 it instead read a general calendar page that did not confirm the event. The system prompt and web guide already said to verify dates and details on pages read, so these were failures to apply visible instructions. It also did not save the volunteered stable location as a memory after the empty memory search at step 1.

- `context:web/guide` (0.96): The guide says to read pages and check details, but does not explicitly require that the cited page identify the same event being recommended. This allowed a different event’s calendar link and a mismatched search result to be treated as confirmation.

Check the event name, date, time, and location on the page itself; search snippets and general calendar pages are not enough to confirm those details. If a result’s title conflicts with its snippet, a page shows a different event, or the page does not confirm a detail, do not present that detail as confirmed. Link the exact page you read that supports the recommendation, or omit the recommendation.
- `context:hub/memory` (0.78): The memory guidance says to remember lasting facts and preferences, but the assistant did not retain the volunteered location after finding no existing memory.
  > When someone voluntarily shares a stable personal fact or lasting preference that is likely to help in future chats—such as their home area or a recurring preference—save a brief memory with user scope, unless they ask you not to. Do not save temporary details that only apply to the current task, sensitive information, or guesses. Say that you saved something only after the memory tool confirms it.

**Request:** "Is it worth getting a heat pump where I live?"

**Good:** Asks location and current heating, cites real sources, gives a straight answer.

Mean 7.7/10 · verdicts differ · $0.105

### rep 1: pass 9/10

The assistant got the needed home details and gave the requested straight “it depends” answer, with a clear recommendation and relevant, linked sources. It was appropriately cautious about savings and incentives rather than treating the winter gas bill as enough to calculate a payoff.

- ✓ Asked for location and current heating/AC details before making a personalized recommendation.
- ✓ Gave a clear bottom line: consider a heat pump when replacing the old AC, but retain the gas furnace as backup and don’t assume guaranteed bill savings.
- ✓ Cited relevant ENERGY STAR, DOE, IRS, and Ohio sources and noted the limits of what they establish.

3 turns · 71 runs · 15 model calls · hub $0.0373 · person $0.0007 · 97s · ended: satisfied (Got the straight it-depends answer with reasons and real sources, no more questions, so nothing left to ask.)

**Diagnosis:** The assistant largely followed the right path: it checked for a remembered location, asked for the ZIP code, loaded web guidance, researched and read relevant sources, and gave the requested qualified answer without asking another question after the person said not to. The avoidable detour came at step 5, where it used `hub__fns_search` for facts even though `web__search` was available, and at steps 6 and 11, where it repeated tool or guide discovery after those were already available. The substantive wording issue is step 15: the sources and user details establish that the AC is 15 years old, but do not establish that replacement is already necessary; “You’re already facing an AC replacement” turns a possibility into a fact.

- `system-prompt` (0.94): The model used `hub__fns_search` to look for web facts and repeated tool and guide discovery even though the web tools and `web/guide` were already available.
  > Choose the search tool by what you are looking for: use `web__search` to find public webpages and `web__read` to check a page; use `hub__fns_search` only to find callable tools. Before using a system, load its guide once. If the guide is already in your prompt and the needed tool is already available, use them directly; do not search for or load them again.
- `system-prompt` (0.86): The answer turned an age-based inference into the factual claim “You’re already facing an AC replacement,” although neither the person nor the cited results established that replacement was necessary.
  > Separate stated facts from inferences. Do not present a likely condition, need, or planned action as established unless the person or a tool result confirms it. When advice depends on an inference, label it as a possibility and make the recommendation conditional—for example, “If replacement is approaching…” rather than saying replacement is already needed.

> **Probably worth considering in Columbus—but the financial case depends on what you’re replacing.**

A **dual-fuel system**—heat pump plus your existing gas furnace—can keep the furnace for the coldest periods or when gas is cheaper to run.
> 
> The economics are less clear if you already have a working gas furnace: electricity and gas prices, the furnace’s efficiency, and the installed price all matter. For context, Columbia Gas’s November 2026 SCO gas *commodity* price is $0.5067/Ccf, but that is only one part of the gas bill, so it can’t be compared directly with an electric rate. > **Yes—Columbus is a reasonable place to get a heat pump, especially when replacing both your furnace and air conditioner. But if your main goal is to cut bills while keeping a working natural-gas furnace, probably not.**
> 
> Why:
> 
> - **Climate:** Heat pumps can handle Columbus winters, but cold-weather performance matters. ENERGY STAR’s “Cold Climate” designation requires a model to retain at least 70% of its 47°F heating capacity at 5°F, with a coefficient of performance of at least 1.75 at 5°F. Look for that designation and have the system sized for your home.
> - **Running costs:** Electricity prices make the comparison important. EIA reports Ohio residential electricity at **19.09¢/kWh in September 2026**. A Columbus-area comparison using its stated utility-rate assumptions finds gas heat cheaper per unit of delivered heat than a heat pump for many homes with gas—though that’s an estimate, not a quote for your house.
> - **When it’s more attractive:** If you heat with electric resistance, don’t have gas, or need to replace your AC anyway, a heat pump can make more sense. A **dual-fuel** setup—heat pump plus gas furnace backup—is a sensible option to price if you already have gas.
> 
> **Bottom line:** Get a heat-pump quote when your HVAC is due for replacement; don’t replace a working gas system solely on the assumption that it will lower your heating bills. Ask for a home-specific cost comparison and the system’s output at 5°F.

> - **The bill savings aren’t a sure thing against gas.** Columbia Gas’s November 2026 Standard Choice Offer is **$0.5067 per Ccf for gas supply**; delivery charges and fixed charges are additional. AEP Ohio electricity bills have several components—including generation, distribution, transmission and riders—so the cost comparison depends on your actual rates and the heat pump’s performance. > - **The upfront cost matters.** A heat pump can also provide air conditioning, which improves the case if your AC is due for replacement too. But I wouldn’t assume energy-bill savings alone will repay an early replacement.
> - **Don’t count on the federal home-improvement tax credit for a 2026 installation:** the IRS says that credit applied to qualifying improvements made through December 31, 2025. [IRS credit details](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/energy-efficient-home-improvement-credit)
>

When you’re ready to replace the system, get bids for both a high-efficiency gas furnace and a cold-climate heat pump (including dual-fuel), and compare them using your actual utility bills.
